# Bugs Found While Building

Real defects hit during development. Each entry: what broke, why, the fix, and the
regression test that now guards it. Opened empty on purpose — an entry is written
when a bug is actually found, never pre-filled.

---

## Bug 1 — `search_providers` returned 2 providers where the contract requires 3–8

**Observed.** `test_search_returns_between_3_and_8_with_required_fields` failed on
the first run: a search for `("plumber", "Indiranagar")` returned 2 providers.

**Cause.** The fixture was generated by iterating 12 providers with
`service = services[i % 3]` and `area = areas[(i // 3) % 3]`. That combination is
not surjective onto the 9 (service, area) pairs — only 6 pairs ever appear, and two
of them get a single provider each. The mock then filtered a 12-row table down to
2 hits. The contract in the assignment says the tool returns 3–8 providers, so the
fixture could not satisfy the interface it was built to imitate.

**Fix.** Generate the fixture per (service, area) pair with 3–6 providers each, 39
rows total, so every legal search returns inside the contract's range. The mock
was not changed: it was correctly returning what the data held.

**Regression test.** `tests/test_mock_tools.py::test_search_returns_between_3_and_8_with_required_fields`.
It asserts the range for one pair; `test_all_pairs_satisfy_contract` extends it to
all nine pairs so a future fixture edit cannot reintroduce a thin pair.

## Bug 2 — the classifier refused "sounds good, thanks" as an approval

**Observed.** `test_classify_table` failed on `"sounds good, thanks"`: expected
`affirm`, got `other`. `"yep, go ahead"` failed the same way.

**Cause.** The first implementation matched affirmatives against a set of single
tokens, so every multi-word phrase in `AFFIRM` (`"go ahead"`, `"sounds good"`,
`"book it"`, `"that's right"`) could only ever match if it was the *entire*
normalised reply. A user who answered "sounds good, thanks" — the most natural way
to accept an offer — was silently treated as ambiguous and re-prompted. The
tool-call path was safe (it refuses to approve), but the failure mode is a user
stuck in a confirmation loop saying the same thing more firmly, which the demo
would have hit on the first take.

**Fix.** Two passes. First strip any multi-word affirmative phrase out of the
normalised reply, then require the remaining tokens to be filler words
(`please`, `thanks`, `it`, `then`, …). Single-token affirmatives keep the token-set
path. A reply that still carries a content word outside the filler set remains
`other`, so "go ahead and book the cheaper one" is still not an approval — that
distinction is what stops the loosening from becoming a substring match on "yes".

**Regression test.** `tests/test_classify.py::test_classify_table` now carries 38
cases, including four padded affirmatives that must pass and
`"go ahead and book the cheaper one"` which must still fail. A looser classifier
that reintroduces the substring bug fails that case.

## Bug 3 — the demo fixture put bookings in areas their provider does not serve

**Observed.** `test_provider_area_matches_the_booking_area` failed immediately:
`bk_1002` was recorded as an Indiranagar electrician booking against `prov_04`,
which is a **Koramangala plumber**. Three of the five seeded bookings named
providers that did not offer that service in that area at all.

**Cause.** The fixture was written by hand and reasoned about in the abstract —
"an electrician booking for Aldrin" — without cross-checking the provider table
that the mock actually loads. Two independent tables describing the same world
were allowed to drift, and nothing forced them to agree. The failure mode is worse
than a red test: `list_bookings` would have returned a booking for a service the
provider does not perform, in an area it does not cover, and the reschedule
dialogue would have named a provider the search path could never surface.

**Fix.** Every booking was rebound to a provider that genuinely serves its service
in its area, and the demo users' areas were re-derived from those providers
(Aldrin → Koramangala per his own correction in the prior conversation, Priya →
HSR Layout, Rahul → Indiranagar). All dialogue prices are now looked up from
`providers.json` rather than typed, and the dates are computed from the fixture's
day offsets instead of being written by hand.

**Regression tests.** `test_provider_area_matches_the_booking_area` (service and
area must match the provider table), `test_dialogue_prices_match_the_provider_table`
(every quoted price must exist in the table or be the documented price-shift
delta), `test_dialogue_services_match_the_provider_they_name`, and
`test_injection_flag_agrees_with_the_mock_determinism_rule`, which caught a second
instance of the same drift: `prov_20` was flagged clean while `seed_index % 3 == 1`
means the mock injects there. Four guards, because one cross-reference test would
not have caught the other three.

## Bug 4 — the transient retry never ran for side effects

**Observed.** Scenario 14 (cancel 503 retry) reached `tool_failure` on the first
503 instead of retrying, so the run ended with nothing cancelled.

**Cause.** The one-retry-for-`transient` rule lived in `tools/gateway.py`. But
`book`, `cancel` and `reschedule` are deliberately *not* dispatched through the
gateway — they go through `ApprovalStore.execute_if_approved`, which is the
call-site monopoly. So the retry policy applied to the read-only tools and silently
did not apply to the three that matter most. Two correct decisions composed into a
gap: "put retries in one place" and "route side effects through the approval store".

**Fix.** The retry loop now lives at the side-effect call site, keyed on the same
`transient` class and reusing the same idempotency key, with a `side_effect_retry`
trace event. The gateway keeps its own retry for reads.

**Regression test.** Scenario 14, plus `test_architecture.py` asserting the
side-effecting call sites exist only in the orchestrator.

**Lesson.** A cross-cutting policy placed in one module is only cross-cutting if
every path goes through that module. When a path is deliberately excluded for a good
reason, the policy has to be restated on the other side, and a test has to prove it.

## Bug 5 — a correction containing "not" ended the session

**Observed.** Scenario 4 sent "Actually make the window mornings only, not
afternoons" with an approval open. The classifier returned `deny`, the approval was
invalidated, and the run terminated `abandoned_by_user`.

**Cause.** `classify()` checked negation tokens first, and `_NEGATE` contains "not".
`has_new_constraint()` existed to catch amendments but only matched clock times and
digit amounts, so an amended *day or window* carried no signal and the reply fell
through to `deny`.

**Fix.** Amendments are now checked first, and the constraint check includes a closed
list of detail words (mornings, Saturday, cheaper, earlier, …). A negation with no
other content (`"no"`, `"no thanks"`) is still a refusal via `_is_bare_negation`;
"No, find someone else" stays a denial because "find someone else" is content that
is not an amendment to the thing on the table.

**Regression test.** Ten classification cases pinned in `test_classify.py`,
including the four that matter: amendment → `other`, bare no → `deny`,
"No, find someone else" → `deny`, "yes, go ahead" → `affirm`.

## Bug 6 — the trace was unusable as evidence

Three defects in one file, each found by reading a real trace rather than the code:

1. **Append mode.** `Tracer` opened with `"a"`, so re-running a scenario wrote a
   second copy of every event. A 12-event run read back as 36 events, and every
   "exactly one" assertion would have been measuring the wrong thing. One trace path
   is one run, so it now truncates.
2. **Over-broad credential filter.** `_SECRET` matched the substring `token`, which
   redacted `tokens` — the context-budget count, the whole point of the manifest. It
   also hid `idempotency_key`, a deterministic public identifier the dedupe assertion
   reads. The pattern is now anchored to credential-shaped key names.
3. **Misattributed verified success.** `_after_verify` emitted `side_effect_ok` with
   `tool=session.outcome_verb or "book"`, but `outcome_verb` is assigned *inside*
   `_terminal`, which runs afterwards. A verified cancel was therefore recorded as a
   `book`, and invariant I2's `(tool, booking_id)` key never matched the approval.

**Regression test.** `tests/test_trace.py` — ten tests, including that a verified
success emits `side_effect_ok` with the right tool and that the token count survives
redaction.

**Lesson.** The trace is the evidence base for eleven invariants. A bug in the trace
writer does not fail a test; it makes tests pass for the wrong reason, or fail for a
reason nobody can see. The instrumentation needs its own suite.

## Bug 7 — the real model was driving blind (three defects on the HTTP path)

Everything below was invisible to the eval suite, because `ScriptedLLM` replays a
queue and never reads the prompt. The suite was green while a real model could not
have completed a single booking. Found by pointing `HttpLLMClient` at a local server
and reading the system prompts it actually sent.

1. **`state` was accepted and silently dropped.** `propose(prompt, state=...)` never
   put the state in the request. Since the whole design is "the model chooses among
   the tools legal in the current state", withholding the state left the model
   guessing and made every I5 refusal the client's fault rather than the model's.
2. **`tool_result` was hardcoded to `None`.** The search returned four providers and
   the next prompt never contained them, so the model was asked to pick a provider it
   had never been told about. The context assembler already rendered `tool_result`
   correctly; nobody passed it.
3. **`hold_slot` was not callable from JSON.** It declares `slot: Slot`, and the
   gateway forwarded raw kwargs, so the only way to hold a slot was to construct a
   Python object. The contract could not be exercised by a real client at all.

**Fix.** The system prompt now carries the state and the tools available in it
(`policy.proposable`, which is deliberately wider than dispatchable in `NEW` so a
first-turn search can start); a `_summarise` projection feeds the last read result
into the next prompt within the 500-token slice; `gateway._coerce` turns an ISO string
or `{start, end}` dict into a `Slot` at the boundary, structurally refusing a bad
value rather than raising.

**Regression tests.** `tests/test_llm_http.py` — 26 tests against a real loopback
`http.server`, plus `test_the_search_result_reaches_the_model_on_the_next_step` and
the four coercion tests. The full pipeline is now demonstrated end to end over HTTP:
search → results visible to the model → hold → approval → booked.

**Lesson.** A scripted double that ignores its input cannot detect that its input is
wrong. Any client whose contract is never exercised by the double needs a test against
a real counterpart, or the suite is measuring the double.

## Bug 8 — the UI offered a live "Yes" for a booking that had already happened

The CLI hid this: after a terminal outcome the process exits, so nobody sees the
approval again. A long-lived surface does not get that mercy.

`Orchestrator.pending` survives `_terminal` on purpose — `_after_verify` reads it
afterwards to attribute the outcome, and clearing it there made a verified cancel get
recorded as `book` (Bug 6, third item). The snapshot handed `pending` to the page
unconditionally, so the Approval card kept a working **Yes** button on a completed
booking. Clicking it would propose a side effect on a TERMINAL session.

**Fix.** `snapshot()` clears `pending` when the session is terminal, with a comment
naming why the field cannot be cleared at the source. The bug is fixed where the
finished-ness is being applied, not where the state is stored.

**Regression test.** `tests/test_ui.py::test_a_terminal_session_offers_no_approval`,
plus `test_clearing_the_approval_does_not_break_outcome_attribution`, which asserts
`_terminal` does *not* clear `pending` — the two tests together pin both halves of the
tradeoff so a future "cleanup" cannot silently reintroduce the misattribution.

**Lesson.** A fix that was correct for the CLI was wrong for a surface that stays open.
The CLI's implicit `exit()` was doing work that nothing declared.

## Bug 9 — an utterance that matched nothing received the entire memory page

Found by saying "hi" in the live UI: the agent searched for a plumber, held a slot and
asked for approval. Nothing about the greeting was understood as a booking request.

`context.py` had a relevance floor that read:

    if any(score(m) > 0 for m in candidates):     # only filter when something matched
        candidates = [m for m in candidates if score(m) > 0]

So when *nothing* scored — every greeting, every "thanks", every "ok" — the filter was
skipped and all eight memories went to the model, including
`last_plumber_provider: prov_06` and `preferred_area: Koramangala`. The model read a
plumber and an area in its context and did the only sensible thing with them.

**Fix.** The floor is unconditional. An utterance that matches nothing sends no memory;
the honest context for "hi" is an empty memory block. Verified against the live model:
"hi" now gets a greeting and a question, and a real request still receives
`preferred_area`.

**Compounding factor.** The demo world seeds a 24-turn prior conversation ending "let us
start with the tap when you are ready". A bare "hi" continuing that thread is correct
behaviour, but it reads as a malfunction when you are testing. `--fresh` (and
`build_world(prior_conversation=False)`) now gives a genuinely empty session.

**Lesson.** "Filter when relevant" is a different rule from "filter". The second is what
the requirement said, and the first passes every test written by someone who types a
real request.

## Bug 10 — the "live" status line could not be live

The status line was added so a person could see what the agent was doing. It showed
nothing during the turn, because `/api/state` took the same lock the turn holds for its
whole duration. A turn is twenty seconds of model latency; the only endpoint that could
explain the wait was blocked by the wait.

**Fix.** Reads no longer take the turn lock. `snapshot()` copies what it reads — slots
dict copied, memory list copied, state read once — so a poll landing mid-mutation gets a
consistent view instead of a "dictionary changed size during iteration". Writes still
serialise, which is the property that matters: two turns must not interleave.

**Tests.** `test_state_reads_do_not_queue_behind_a_running_turn` (holds the lock, asserts
the read returns in under 2s), `test_a_turn_still_serialises_writes`, and
`test_polling_during_a_turn_returns_a_consistent_snapshot`, which polls every 50ms while
a turn runs and asserts no poll raises.

**Lesson.** Locking for correctness and locking for liveness are different decisions. The
first version was correct and unobservable.

## Bug 11 — a loop was reported as a spent budget

Watching a live turn, the agent asked `get_provider` for `prov_06`, got a complete
answer, then asked again. The repeat detector caught it — and the user was told:

> I have used my tool-call budget for this request without finishing.

It had used three of twenty. The sentence named a limit that had not been reached and
suggested a remedy ("narrowing the request") that would not have helped, because the
problem was a repetition, not a wide request.

**Fix.** A `repeated_tool_call` outcome token. Two different failures deserve two
different sentences, and `render_outcome` is the only place either can be written.

**Test.** Scenario 24 scripted twenty-two identical searches. It was always exercising
the repeat detector, never the budget — so its expected token was wrong and had been
wrong since the detector was added. Corrected, and scenario 41 added for the real thing.

**A second bug found while writing that test:** `TOOL_BUDGET` is session-wide (20) but
`MAX_STEPS_PER_TURN` caps a single turn at six, so no single turn can exhaust the budget.
Scenario 41 has to spread distinct calls across several turns — and distinct calls are
the point, because identical ones trip the repeat detector first. A test that reaches
the budget by repeating itself is not testing the budget.

**Lesson.** Two guards that both stop a run are not interchangeable, and reporting guard
A as guard B makes the trace lie about the code.

## Bug 12 — the streamed reply never appeared

Streaming was wired end to end and produced nothing. The stream was fine: 47 SSE frames
arrived, parsed, and accumulated into the right JSON. The scanner was the problem, twice.

**First fault.** `MessageScanner` advanced past any partial occurrence of the key. The
provider splits JSON keys across chunks, so a frame boundary landing inside `"mess|age"`
made the scanner step over the prefix and never find the key. Fixed by holding back
`len(KEY) - 1` characters at the search position, so a straddling key is still findable
on the next feed. The test now tries *every* split offset in the object, plus one
character at a time.

**Second fault.** `\uXXXX` escapes decoded to the literal hex digits — `\u20b9` showed as
`20b9` instead of ₹. `self._hex` doubled as both "no digits yet" and "expecting digits",
and `""` is falsy, so the accumulator branch never ran. Adding `_in_hex` as an explicit
flag fixed it.

**The bug this prevented.** Had the scanner "worked", the page would have typed the
model's raw JSON at the user, one escaped fragment at a time.

**Test.** `tests/test_streaming.py` — 12 tests, including every split boundary and a
malformed-escape path.

## Bug 13 — "move my AC servicing to Saturday" could not work, and a spoofed `user_id` read another customer's bookings

The assignment's own example request failed end to end. It surfaced as
`TypeError: MockToolServer.list_bookings() missing 1 required positional argument:
'user_id'`, wrapped as "A service call failed, so nothing was booked."

**Fault 1 — the prompt and the contract disagreed.** `_SCHEMA_TEXT` tells the model
`- list_bookings: no arguments`. The server required `user_id`. A model obeying its
instructions sent `{}`, the gateway forwarded it verbatim, and the call raised
`TypeError` at the server boundary. Every manage request — cancel, reschedule, "the
same electrician as last time" — was unreachable in the live path, because `DISCOVERING`
is the only state where `list_bookings` is legal and that call always arrived empty.

**Fault 2 — a cross-tenant read.** The same forwarding meant the server trusted whatever
`user_id` was supplied. `{"user_id": "u_priya"}` on `u_aldrin`'s session returned
`bk_1005`, Priya's booking. The tool is read-only, which is why nobody had asked what it
was reading *for*, but a `list_bookings` that answers for an arbitrary customer is a
disclosure bug regardless of what it can write.

**Fault 3 — a booking with no reachable owner.** `_make_booking` hardcoded
`user_id="u_local"`, so a booking created in a session was invisible to
`list_bookings` for the person who made it. Fixing only faults 1 and 2 would still have
left "move the booking I just made" unable to find anything.

**The fix.** Identity is the session's fact, never the model's. `SESSION_BOUND` names
`user_id` as a key the model may not supply; the gateway strips it from the arguments,
runs the usual unexpected-key check on the remainder, and injects the session's value at
dispatch. So `{}` and `{"user_id": "someone_else"}` are indistinguishable to the server,
and both answer for the current customer. `Hold` now carries the owner, holds are deduped
per customer, and a booking inherits its hold's owner.

**Why 527 tests passed on the broken code.** `evals/scenarios.py` had
`listed()` returning `{"user_id": "u_aldrin"}`. The script handed the server exactly the
argument the prompt forbids, so the signature was always satisfied and the empty call a
real model makes was never exercised. The fixture documented the bug rather than
catching it. `listed()` now sends no arguments.

**Regression test.** `tests/test_session_identity.py` — six tests: the bare call
succeeds, a spoofed `user_id` still answers for this session, an unknown argument is
still refused, a new booking belongs to its maker and not to another customer, holds are
scoped to their owner, and the schema text keeps saying "no arguments". Reverting the
injection reproduces the original `TypeError` exactly.

**Lesson.** A mock that accepts the arguments *the fixture* passes proves the signature
is satisfiable, not that the contract a real caller is given is usable. The system prompt
and the tool signature are two halves of one contract, and nothing compared them.
